title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [MacRumors] New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

As confirmed by the website "Expand Mac mini," NAND storage in the new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips is soldered to the logic board, whereas the previous models with the M4 and M4 Pro chips have removable storage that can be upgraded.


In other words, the new Mac mini does not support aftermarket storage upgrades.

"Expand Mac mini" offers plug-and-play SSD modules that are functionally equivalent to Apple's proprietary modules, yet hundreds of dollars cheaper. As a result, customers were able to save a significant amount of money by configuring their Mac mini with the minimum 256GB capacity that was available on Apple's online store and later installing a higher-capacity aftermarket module. With the new models, that is no longer possible.

"We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely," the "Expand Mac mini" website said, in a blog post.

Mac mini models with the M1 chip and M2/M2 Pro chips also had NAND soldered to the logic board, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations having removable storage has proven to be a one-off exception for now. Apple has not commented on the reversal.

In addition, all new Mac mini configurations with 256GB of storage reportedly have a single NAND chip, rather than a pair of 128GB chips. As a result, 256GB configurations have slower SSD speeds compared to configurations with 512GB of storage or more that do have dual NAND chips, according to AAPL Ch.'s testing with Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool.






















Mac mini Configuration Read Speed Write Speed
M6, 512GB 6,371.5 MB/s 6,577.4 MB/s
M6, 256GB 3,216.8 MB/s 3,000.2 MB/s
M4, 256GB 2,792.5 MB/s 2,014.5 MB/s



The new 256GB model's Disk Speed Test scores were roughly half that of models with 512GB of storage or more. The average customer is unlikely to notice the difference, but power users will appreciate knowing that they need to opt for at least 512GB of storage in order to achieve the fastest SSD speeds possible.

Fortunately, even with 256GB of storage, it appears that the new Mac mini has meaningfully faster SSD speeds compared to the previous 256GB model.

Mac mini models with M2/M2 Pro and 256GB of storage also had a single NAND chip, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations proved to be a one-off exception for this too.

items.content_html:

Scientists say changing clouds and increasingly thin ice may explain the pause, but continued Arctic warming could eventually trigger another period of rapid change.
